title: The road of lying
hookLine: truthfulness leads to goodness, lying to wickedness (Bukhari)

cards: A road doesn't have to be steep to take you somewhere. One step, then the next, and an hour later you're in another town without ever deciding to move there. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes two roads like that.
On one, a person keeps telling the truth. On the other, a person keeps lying. Neither looks dramatic from the first step.
Both arrive somewhere. Today, the next disease on the path: the road of lying.

teach.b: Here is the hadith, in plain English. Truthfulness leads to goodness, and goodness leads to the garden.

A person keeps telling the truth until he is written with Allah as truthful. And lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the fire. A person keeps lying until he is written with Allah as a liar.
Notice the word keeps. It's about which road the feet are used to. Second, how small the steps can be.
In a report in Sunan Abu Dawud, a mother calls her little boy over: come here, I'll give you something. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is in the house and asks what she meant to give him.
Some dates, she says. And he tells her that if she'd given him nothing, it would have been written against her as a lie. A coaxing line to a child.
In Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful." Truth is easier to walk with others.
And last, a reading some teachers offer: under several of these diseases sits a small lie the heart tells. I'm better. They don't deserve it.
Watch me. I'm owed. Not enough.
Did you hear what she did. The road of truth starts with telling yourself the truth first.

how: Muslims are taught truthfulness, sidq, as a habit that leads to goodness, following the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari; teachers warn against small lies too, including the coaxing lies told to children.

games.q: what does “the road of lying” mean?
o: being honest about painful things too bluntly
one single big lie that ruins your life for good
lie after lie, a habit that leads to wickedness

games.q: the road of lying — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith is about one big lie
it's about a person who keeps lying, or keeps telling the truth: a road, a habit.
a coaxing line to a child, with nothing behind it, would be written as a lie
the report in Sunan Abu Dawud: she meant to give him dates, so it wasn't.
the Qur'an tells believers to be with the truthful
"Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful."

games.q: a mother calls her little boy: 'come here, I'll give you something.' the Prophet asks what she meant to give. what does he say about it?
o: it's only a child, so it doesn't matter.
if she'd meant to give nothing, it would be written as a lie.
promises to children should never be made.
games.why: she said dates, and he told her that if she'd given him nothing, it would have been written against her as a lie.

practice: Walk through the day ahead and find where the small ones usually live: I'm five minutes away, I love it, I didn't see your message.

Choose a true version now, kind and short: I'm running late, it's not for me but thank you, I saw it and needed time. If you pray, you can ask to be written among the truthful; if not, just hold the true sentence ready.

wordCard.voice: The road of lying. The hadith's picture of habit: lie after lie leads to wickedness, and truth after truth leads to goodness and the garden. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: truthfulness, the first road in the hadith.

carryVoice: Your line: truth leads to good. The word that matters is keeps. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful.
